practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a mechanical building service?
A) Smoke detection systems
B) IT network cabling
C) Air conditioning
D) Stormwater drainage
practice_questions.marks: C) Air conditioning [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two examples of infrastructure and civil engineering products that the construction sector is responsible for building.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: roads / railways / bridges / tunnels / water supply and sewerage systems / electrical grids / telecommunications. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a residential building and a non-residential building, giving one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Residential: used as a place where people live (1 mark); example such as house / flat / apartment block (1 mark). Non-residential: a building that serves a purpose other than housing people (1 mark); example such as office / school / hospital / factory (1 mark). Maximum 3 marks — credit the clearest three points made. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the function of public health building services in a new school building.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Credit: cold water supply — brings fresh drinking water to taps and toilets (1); domestic hot water system — heats water for sinks and showers (1); wastewater/sewage drainage — removes used water from sinks and toilets to the sewer (1); stormwater drainage — collects rainwater from roofs/playgrounds to prevent flooding (1). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A construction company has been awarded a contract to build a large railway tunnel under a city centre.

Explain why this type of project would be classified as infrastructure and civil engineering rather than a building project.
practice_questions.marks: Infrastructure/civil engineering refers to large-scale systems and networks (1) that underpin the functioning of society (1). A railway tunnel is not a building — it has no enclosed habitable space — but instead allows trains to travel underground (1), connecting communities and enabling the movement of people and freight on a wide scale (1). Accept other valid reasoning about scale, purpose or classification. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A large hospital is being refurbished. The project manager is responsible for coordinating the installation of mechanical, electrical and public health services throughout the building.

Discuss the importance of building services engineering to the users of the hospital.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies all three categories with developed explanation applied to a hospital context. For example: mechanical services — lifts are essential for moving patients and equipment between floors; ventilation and air conditioning maintain sterile conditions to prevent infection (developed point). Electrical services — fire detection protects vulnerable patients; energy supply powers medical equipment and lighting in operating theatres (developed point). Public health services — clean water supply is critical for hygiene and patient care; wastewater drainage prevents contamination (developed point). Recognises that these systems interact and that failure of any one could be life-threatening in a hospital.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two categories identified with some explanation applied to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two relevant points with limited application.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant statement. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of a stonemason?
A) Laying bricks in mortar using traditional bonding patterns
B) Dressing, carving and laying natural stone, including dry-stone walling
C) Applying levelling compounds and laying carpet and vinyl floor finishes
D) Installing cold water, hot water and central heating systems
practice_questions.marks: B) Dressing, carving and laying natural stone, including dry-stone walling [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two tasks carried out by a plasterer on a construction project.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct tasks from: applying render to external walls / applying plaster to inside walls and ceilings / dry lining internal stud walls (plasterboard) / replicating traditional ornamental plasterwork using moulds and casts. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a joiner and a carpenter.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that they are different roles (e.g. "they are separate trades"). A second mark for explaining the joiner's role (e.g. "a joiner works in a workshop, joining pieces of wood to make components such as doors, window frames or staircases"). A third mark for explaining the carpenter's role (e.g. "a carpenter works on site, installing the components made by the joiner and also fitting structural elements such as floor joists, floorboards and roof trusses"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the work of an electrician on a new-build house, including one safety regulation they must follow.
practice_questions.marks:
Description of work (up to 3 marks): installs, inspects and tests electrical services and equipment; runs cables and fits consumer units (fuse boards); wires sockets, switches and lighting circuits; may install specialist equipment such as security systems or fire alarms (one mark per distinct point, up to 3).
Safety requirement (1 mark): for example, works competently and follows relevant safety requirements; BS 7671 is a widely used standard for electrical installations. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A construction firm is building a new residential estate. The site manager notices that gas boilers need to be fitted, but the assigned plumber is not Gas Safe registered.

Explain why this is a problem and what action the site manager should take.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear explanation that Gas Safe registration is a legal requirement for anyone working on gas appliances or pipework in the UK; using an unregistered person is illegal, creates serious safety risks (including carbon monoxide poisoning, gas leaks or explosion), and could expose the employer to legal liability. The site manager should stop the plumber from carrying out any gas work immediately and arrange for a Gas Safe registered engineer to carry out the installation. Marks also available for noting that the site manager is responsible for safety on site and may be held to account for breaches.
Secure (3-4 marks): Recognises Gas Safe as a legal requirement, identifies safety risks and states an appropriate action.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies Gas Safe as important but limited explanation of why.
Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A historic manor house is being restored. The project requires bricklayers, stonemasons, carpenters and painters and decorators.

Evaluate the importance of each trade working from plans and specifications on this type of project, compared with a standard new-build.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A developed evaluation covering how plans and specifications ensure trades coordinate their work (e.g. carpenter's components are sized to fit the stonemason's openings; painter's specification details heritage-approved finishes). On a heritage project this is especially important because materials and methods must match the existing fabric of the building, comply with planning conditions, and often satisfy conservation requirements — errors are harder and more expensive to correct than on a standard new-build. Counter-argument: on a standard new-build the same framework applies but tolerances are less critical and materials are more standardised. Substantiated judgement: following plans and specifications is critical on all projects, but the consequences of deviation are more severe on a heritage project. Quality of written communication should be credited.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two trades discussed with some comparison of heritage vs new-build.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points, largely descriptive.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which professional association represents architects in the UK?
A) CIOB
B) RICS
C) RIBA
D) HSE
practice_questions.marks: C) RIBA [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two responsibilities of a site manager during a construction project.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: coordinating construction site activities / managing progress and site meetings / organising resources of labour, plant and materials / undertaking day-to-day activities / being responsible for health and safety and worker welfare. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between the role of a surveyor and the role of a quantity surveyor.
practice_questions.marks: Surveyor: measures land and existing features / sets out construction works on site from drawings / produces data and drawings for architects and engineers (1 mark for one relevant point, 2 marks for two clearly distinct points). Quantity surveyor: manages the financial aspects of a project / makes payments to subcontractors / produces a final account / controls budgets and costs (1 mark). Maximum 3 marks — reward a clear contrast. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two benefits of membership of a professional association such as RICS or CIOB for a construction professional.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for each benefit described with development (up to 4 marks). Examples: access to CPD — training and development resources that keep skills current and help maintain professional standards (2 marks); professional recognition — chartered status signals to employers and clients that the individual meets recognised standards, which is particularly important when winning competitive contracts (2 marks); professional network — access to peers who share knowledge, job opportunities and industry updates (2 marks). Accept other valid benefits with development. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A large office development is under construction. The architect has produced the design, and work on site has begun.

Explain the roles of the contracts manager and the quantity surveyor during the construction stage of this project.
practice_questions.marks: Contracts manager (up to 2 marks): coordinates site activities and manages progress (1); organises labour, plant and materials and is responsible for health and safety on site (1). Quantity surveyor (up to 2 marks): controls the project budget and monitors costs against forecast (1); checks and processes payments to subcontractors and suppliers (1). Accept other correct responsibilities. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A civil engineering company is tendering for a large public infrastructure contract. The project will involve designing a new road bridge, managing site operations and controlling a budget of several million pounds.

Discuss the professional roles that would be needed on this project and explain how they would work together to deliver it successfully.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies at least four roles with distinct responsibilities and explains how they interact. For example: architect/designer creates the design for the bridge to meet planning and client requirements; civil and structural engineer produces the structural design compliant with British Standards and assesses risks such as load capacity and foundation depth; contracts manager/site manager oversees site operations, manages workers and equipment, and maintains health and safety; quantity surveyor controls the multi-million pound budget, processes payments and produces a final account. The answer explains how these roles work together — e.g. the engineer's design informs the QS cost plan; the architect checks the contractor's work against the design during construction.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least three roles described with some explanation of interaction.
Developing (2 marks): Two roles named with limited description.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a specific risk assessment on a construction site?
A) A general check of all site access routes and emergency exits
B) An assessment of manual handling tasks involved in lifting heavy concrete blocks
C) A review of the site's overall fire evacuation procedure
D) An inspection of the site perimeter fencing
practice_questions.marks: B) An assessment of manual handling tasks involved in lifting heavy concrete blocks [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two risks that employees face on a construction site.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: heavy plant and construction vehicles / working at height / manual handling / slips, trips and falls. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why employers on a construction site must follow the hierarchy of control when selecting control measures.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that the hierarchy of control is a priority order for selecting control measures. A second mark for explaining the principle (e.g. it requires employers to try to eliminate or reduce the hazard at source before relying on less reliable measures). A third mark for development (e.g. PPE is at the bottom of the hierarchy because it relies on individual workers wearing it correctly at all times, which cannot be guaranteed, whereas engineering controls such as guarding protect everyone automatically). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe employer health and safety duties on a construction project.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any four distinct duties from: prepare risk assessments / decide on control measures / prevent or control exposure to hazards / ensure the hierarchy of control is followed / monitor exposure to hazards / prepare procedures to deal with accidents / train and supervise employees. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Workers on a construction site are cutting stone blocks using dry angle grinders. The site manager has not carried out a COSHH assessment for this task.

Explain the risks this creates and what the site manager should do to comply with COSHH regulations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies the specific hazardous substance (silica dust / respirable crystalline silica released when cutting stone); explains the health risk (silicosis — irreversible lung scarring, lung cancer); explains why the absence of a COSHH assessment is a legal breach; states what the site manager must do (carry out a COSHH assessment identifying RCS as a hazard and implement control measures such as wet cutting, on-tool extraction ventilation, and appropriate PPE such as FFP3 dust masks). Marks also available for noting that COSHH sits alongside the Health and Safety at Work Act and that the employer can be prosecuted for non-compliance.
Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies the hazardous substance, names the health risk and states one or more appropriate actions.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies a hazardous substance or health risk but limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A new housing development site has had three accidents in one month: a worker slipped on a wet walkway, a delivery driver struck a worker near the site entrance, and a labourer sustained a back injury lifting heavy blocks.

Evaluate how effective risk assessments and the correct hierarchy of control could have prevented these accidents.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Analyses each accident in terms of the risk assessment process and hierarchy of control. For slips/trips: a general site risk assessment should have identified wet walkways; control measures higher in the hierarchy than PPE (e.g. non-slip matting, drainage channels, clear housekeeping rules) should have been implemented before issuing wet-weather footwear. For the vehicle strike: a specific risk assessment for site traffic should have identified pedestrian/vehicle conflict; engineering controls (separate pedestrian and vehicle routes, physical barriers, banksmen) should have been in place. For the manual handling injury: a specific manual handling assessment should have identified the weight and awkwardness of concrete blocks; elimination (using mechanical aids such as a block grab) or reduction (team lifting, reduced block sizes) should have been selected before PPE. A substantiated judgement: well-conducted risk assessments, following the hierarchy from eliminate/substitute down to PPE, would have significantly reduced the likelihood of all three accidents. However, risk assessments are only effective if monitored and enforced — procedures alone are insufficient.
Secure (5-6 marks): Two accidents discussed with reference to risk assessment and hierarchy. Some applied evaluation.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points, mostly descriptive.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the seasoning process for timber?
A) Cutting logs into standard-sized boards
B) Removing excess moisture from cut timber to prevent warping
C) Bonding wood fibres together to make engineered boards
D) Treating timber with a preservative chemical
practice_questions.marks: B) Removing excess moisture from cut timber to prevent warping [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of maintenance that may be carried out on a building during the operation and maintenance stage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: planned and preventive maintenance / cyclical maintenance / emergency or reactive maintenance. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a pre-demolition plan must be produced before a building is demolished.
practice_questions.marks: A pre-demolition plan must be produced to identify hazardous materials (1) such as asbestos that must be safely removed before work starts; to identify live utilities (1) such as electricity, gas and water that must be disconnected; and to assess structural risks (1) such as load-bearing party walls that could collapse if not properly managed. Any three of these reasons score 1 mark each. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how clay is manufactured into bricks.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for the process: natural clay minerals are extracted from the ground (1); the clay is crushed to remove large particles and ensure consistency (1); it is shaped into brick-sized moulds (1); the shaped clay is dried to remove surface moisture (1); and then fired in a kiln at high temperature to harden and strengthen the brick (1). Maximum 4 marks. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A block of flats built in the 1970s is being demolished to make way for a new development. The demolition team has found asbestos insulation in the roof space and the building is still connected to the gas main.

Explain the steps the demolition team must take before the main demolition work can begin.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. The team must produce a pre-demolition plan identifying all hazardous materials and utilities present (1). The asbestos must be assessed and removed using the controls required by the risk assessment; a licensed contractor is required where the work is licensable (1). The gas main (and any other live utilities including electricity and water) must be disconnected by the relevant utility company before demolition begins (1). Site security must be set up to prevent members of the public from entering the site (1). Accept other relevant pre-demolition steps covered in this lesson. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A housing developer has demolished a large Victorian factory. The site has produced thousands of old bricks, steel roof trusses and a large volume of broken concrete.

Discuss the options available for dealing with these demolition materials and evaluate the benefits of reusing or recycling them rather than sending them to landfill.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies all three material types with specific disposal/reuse/recycling options. Old bricks — can be reclaimed, cleaned and resold for use in heritage building projects with little reprocessing; preserves the embodied energy in the original firing process. Steel roof trusses — can be assessed for structural condition; if sound, sections can be reused or, if too damaged, sent for smelting/recycling into new steel products. Broken concrete — can be crushed on site into 20 mm aggregate for use as hardcore fill, reducing the need to quarry new aggregate. Benefits of reuse/recycling discussed: reduces landfill costs (including landfill tax), preserves natural resources, reduces carbon emissions from new material production, creates employment in recycling, reduces pollution. Some landfill material may be unavoidable (contaminated or mixed waste).
Secure (3-4 marks): Two material types addressed with some benefit discussion.
Developing (2 marks): One material type with limited discussion.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an electrical certification scheme?
A) Gas Safe
B) COSHH
C) NICEIC
D) CIOB
practice_questions.marks: C) NICEIC [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two risks that a worker faces when entering an enclosed space such as a manhole.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: exposure to fumes / reduced oxygen levels / flooding or drowning / fire and explosive atmospheres / entrapment in machinery. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why an employer must train workers in the correct use of PPE, rather than simply providing it.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for stating that PPE only protects the wearer if worn correctly. A second mark for developing this (e.g. a dust mask that is not correctly fitted to the face allows hazardous particles through; a hard hat worn on the back of the head does not protect against falling objects). A third mark for extending the explanation (e.g. training also covers storage and maintenance — PPE that is stored incorrectly or is damaged may be ineffective, and workers must know how and when to replace it). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the safety measures a site manager must put in place before allowing workers to enter an enclosed space.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any four of: carry out a risk assessment identifying the specific hazards in the enclosed space; test the atmosphere using monitoring equipment before entry; provide appropriate PPE such as breathing apparatus if hazardous gases or low oxygen are identified; appoint a trained attendant to remain outside the space throughout; establish rescue arrangements and a rescue plan in advance of entry; ensure workers know how to communicate with the attendant and how to raise an alarm. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A roofing contractor is replacing the roof covering on a two-storey school building. The work will take four weeks. The contractor has told workers to use ladders throughout, without setting up scaffold, to save time and money.

Explain why this approach is unsafe and describe a safer method of access the contractor should use instead.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Explains that using ladders for a four-week roofing project is unsuitable — ladders are only appropriate for short-duration, light work where a three-point contact can be maintained; they do not provide a stable working platform or edge protection for roofing tasks. Identifies the specific risks: falling from the ladder or the roof edge; falling objects landing below; no guardrails or toe-boards protecting workers or people at ground level. Describes a safer method: scaffold with guardrails (handrails and toe-boards) should be erected around the building to give a stable working platform at eaves level; this provides edge protection and prevents falling objects at ground level. Notes that the scaffold must be inspected by a competent person at least every seven days, and that weather conditions must be monitored. Saving time and money does not justify exposing workers to a foreseeable risk of death or serious injury.
Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies that ladders are unsuitable for this task, names a safer access method and gives one or two safety points.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies the hazard but limited explanation of safer alternatives.
Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A maintenance plumber is called to repair a gas boiler and a burst water pipe in the same property. Both jobs involve services that are live before work begins.

Evaluate the safety steps the plumber must take for each job before and during the work, and explain why Gas Safe registration is particularly important for the gas work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Evaluates safety steps for the water repair: isolate water supply at the relevant stop valve before work begins; use appropriate PPE (waterproof clothing, safety footwear); check for secondary risks (e.g. water damage to electrical fittings nearby). Evaluates safety steps for the gas repair: must be Gas Safe registered (it is illegal to carry out gas work without this); isolate the gas supply at the meter or isolation valve before starting; follow appropriate working practices and safety procedures for gas; use appropriate PPE; test for gas leaks on completion before restoring supply. Justifies why Gas Safe registration is particularly important: gas leaks can cause explosions, fires and carbon monoxide poisoning — all potentially fatal — and an unregistered person may lack the training to carry out the work safely or to test the system correctly on completion. The requirement for Gas Safe registration exists in law precisely because the consequences of unsafe gas work are catastrophic. A substantiated judgement: both jobs require isolation and PPE, but the gas job carries a higher risk of catastrophic harm, which is why registration and formal accreditation are legally required rather than merely recommended.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both jobs discussed, Gas Safe explained, some evaluation of relative risk.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points for one or both jobs, mostly descriptive.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a characteristic of residential dwellings?
A) They are used for storing and processing manufactured goods
B) They are among the smallest building types and used as places of habitation
C) They are usually located in retail centres to attract customers
D) They are typically large buildings with high eaves heights
practice_questions.marks: B) They are among the smallest building types and used as places of habitation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two economic benefits that a new infrastructure project, such as a motorway, might bring to the local area.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: creates jobs (in construction and in businesses attracted to the area) / opens the area to new business investment / reduces transport costs for local businesses / cuts journey times, saving money and fuel / increases the value of nearby properties. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a community building and a recreational building, giving one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Community building: used by members of a community / usually located conveniently for the community (1); example such as village hall / library / health centre (1). Recreational building: accommodates leisure, sport and entertainment activities / may be purpose-built or an extension to another building (1); example such as sports centre / cinema / swimming pool (1). Maximum 3 marks for the clearest three points made. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of industrial buildings.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for each characteristic described with development (up to 4 marks). Examples: large buildings adapted to specific functions such as storage, processing or manufacturing (2 marks); may be purpose-built on a modern industrial park or a refurbished older building/site (2 marks); typically have large clear floor areas, high eaves heights and heavy-duty floor slabs to accommodate machinery and racking (2 marks). Accept other valid characteristics. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A new high-speed rail line is being planned that will run through a rural area, connecting two major cities. Local residents are opposed to the project, while the government argues it will transform the economy.

Explain why infrastructure projects like this are often controversial.
practice_questions.marks: Infrastructure projects are controversial because developers, planning authorities and communities must weigh significant benefits against significant drawbacks (1). Economic benefits include connecting cities, reducing journey times and attracting investment (1). However, economic drawbacks include the high cost to taxpayers and potential cost overruns (1). Social and environmental drawbacks for the rural community include construction noise, traffic disruption and loss of natural habitat and countryside (1). Because different groups prioritise different outcomes, reaching agreement is very difficult. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A property developer has been asked to advise on the most appropriate type of building to construct on two different sites: a large vacant plot on the edge of a town centre, and a small plot in the middle of a housing estate.

Discuss what type of building would be most suitable for each site, giving reasons for your recommendations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Edge-of-town site — recommends commercial or industrial building (1) with justification: out-of-town location suits large-footprint commercial buildings such as a retail park or distribution warehouse (1); good road access at the edge of town is important for deliveries and customer parking (1); the appropriate building type depends on the local plan and the site’s constraints (1). Housing estate site — recommends residential or community building (1) with justification: a small plot in a housing estate would be ideal for infill housing, as it fits the character of the area and addresses housing demand (1); alternatively, a small community building such as a health centre or nursery could serve the existing residential community (1). The answer acknowledges that the primary purpose and location should match the building type's typical characteristics.
Secure (3-4 marks): One site addressed well, or both sites with limited justification.
Developing (2 marks): Both sites named but with minimal reasoning.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State one financial benefit of sustainable construction.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: minimising waste / reducing energy consumption / improving water efficiency / reducing operating costs / optimising the life cycle of buildings.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a developer can reduce the impact of construction on natural habitats.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a method (e.g. building tunnels under roads for newts / creating new bat roosts). One mark for explaining how it reduces impact (e.g. allows wildlife to move safely without being harmed by traffic / replaces roosts lost when buildings are demolished).

practice_questions.text: Describe three sustainable materials that could be used in the construction of a new house, stating a different part of the building for each material.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per correctly matched material and building element, up to three. Acceptable examples: wood frame / straw bale walls / reclaimed slate roof / wool insulation in walls or roof / recycled brick walls / timber shingles on roof / steel structural frame.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between re-using and recycling construction waste. Use examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to two marks for re-use: salvaged products put back into service with little or no reprocessing (1 mark); example such as bricks, slates, or steel sections (1 mark). Up to two marks for recycling: waste is processed (e.g. crushing, smelting, sorting, decontamination) before being used again (1 mark); example such as crushed concrete used as aggregate, or smelted metal used in new components (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of developing a brownfield site rather than a greenfield site.
practice_questions.marks: Up to three marks for brownfield: advantages such as existing roads/drainage/services reduce costs (1), regenerates derelict or run-down communities (1), removes environmental health hazards through decontamination (1); disadvantages such as demolition costs (1), decontamination expense (1), possible residual contamination risk (1). Up to three marks for greenfield: advantages such as no demolition or decontamination needed so cheaper to develop (1), cleaner site conditions (1); disadvantages such as new roads and utility connections required (1), loss of green space and farmland (1), legal and planning constraints (1). Credit clear, developed comparative points. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of using sustainable construction methods for both developers and the wider community. Refer to environmental, financial, and social factors in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): Detailed, balanced evaluation covering all three factors with specific examples and clear judgement about relative importance. Secure (5-6): Good coverage of at least two factors with some development; judgement present but may lack full balance. Developing (3-4): Some relevant points on at least two factors; limited development or judgement. Emerging (1-2): Basic points with little development; may address only one factor. Environmental: reducing CO2 emissions, protecting habitats, reducing pollution in water/air/ground, preserving natural resources. Financial: minimising waste and landfill fees, reducing energy bills, lower operating costs over building's life cycle. Social: improved air quality and occupant comfort, regeneration of communities on brownfield land, protected areas preserving quality of life. [8 marks]
